title: Removable media carrying a signed identity attestation
description:
A USB stick is plugged in. On it is a signed statement of identity -- an
attestation minted offline by an authority, verified against the public key
persona-08sz recorded at enrolment.

NOTHING ON THE STICK COMPUTES, AND THAT IS THE DESIGN, NOT A LIMITATION. There
is no private key to hold and nothing to protect on the media. The signature was
made once, by the authority, before the stick ever existed. The daemon's job is
to check it. PRIOR ART: Mark has built this -- login to a Linux box by putting a
signed text file on a USB drive into the slot. It is a known-working pattern,
not a novel mechanism.

NOTHING IN THE TREE DOES THIS. No udev, no mount watching, no USB handling
anywhere. persona-lnaj proposes a FIXED drop directory; removable media is a
transient mount at a path nobody knows in advance, which is the part lnaj does
not model. did_key.rs reads the HIRE_DID_KEYS environment variable -- no file,
no signature. persona-vmpi.2 is did:web, anchored in DNS and HTTPS rather than
in an enrolment signature.

IT CANNOT ANSWER A CHALLENGE, SAME WALL AS persona-qbnm.6. A static signed file
cannot bind to a nonce the daemon generated this second, so
Evidence::binds_to(candidate, challenge) has nothing to bind. But it is NOT in
the same position as tailscale and oidc, and the difference matters: their trust
basis is unverifiable (tailscaled's word) or unverified (a token whose signature
we never check), while this one is a signature we CAN check, against a key the
user deliberately enrolled. The trust basis is strong. It is the FRESHNESS that
is weak, and those are different problems with different answers.

FOLLOW PlatformIdentity, WHICH ALREADY SOLVED THIS SHAPE. It is the one Evidence
variant with no secret and no challenge behind it, where the operating system is
the entire authority; it binds by CONTENT MATCH -- Evidence::binds_to compares
the account it names against the candidate -- and the daemon stamps the instant
itself so nothing can re-date a cached answer. This is structurally identical,
plus a signature, which makes it STRONGER than PlatformIdentity rather than
weaker. Bind by matching the identity in the signed statement to the candidate;
take freshness from the MOUNT EVENT the daemon observed, never from the file,
which is static and says nothing about when.

PLUGGING IT IN IS A PRESENCE OBSERVATION, and it is worth more than it first
looks. Someone was bodily at that USB port at that moment. That is a physical
act at the machine, and the daemon watched it happen rather than being told
about it. It is also a clean illustration of persona-3tly.2, which holds that
PresenceLevel wrongly fuses user presence with user verification: the mount
event establishes that SOMEONE was there, the signature establishes WHICH BADGE
arrived, and nothing here establishes the binding between them -- a stolen stick
presents exactly as a carried one.

TIER CAPS AT IAA2. An enrolled authority vouched, which is what iaa2 means. Not
iaa3, because nothing is hardware-bound: the signed file is a BEARER CREDENTIAL
and a copy of it verifies identically to the original, so possession is not
exclusive possession and the holder cannot tell they have been duplicated. The
cap is about copyability, not about key custody -- there is no key here to
custody.

PROOF COST IS SILENT (persona-jl4j.3). Reading a mounted filesystem and checking
a signature interrupts nobody.

SHIPPABLE IN THREE STAGES, EACH USEFUL ALONE. Do not wait for the last one.
  1. Scan mounted volumes for a well-known relative path and enumerate what is
     there. Candidate only, no enrolment needed, no signature checked. Already
     useful: another attestor may be able to prove that identity.
  2. Verify against an authority enrolled per persona-08sz and emit evidence,
     bound by content match and dated by the mount. This is the step that mints
     a credential.
  3. Notice the unplug.

STAGE 3 IS REAL BUT IT IS THE WEAKEST MEMBER of persona-3tly.6's observed-
departure class. Pulling a CAC removes the signing capability; pulling this
removes only the copy you happened to be reading. Treat it as evidence the
person left, never as evidence the credential became unusable -- it did not,
anywhere a copy exists.

Mounting untrusted removable media is itself a filesystem attack surface, and
the daemon does not choose when it appears. Read the well-known path and nothing
else; do not walk the volume.
acceptance_criteria: Stage 1 alone, merged and useful: a mounted volume with the well-known file yields a Candidate, declared Iaa2-attainable and Silent, proving nothing. Stage 2 binds by content match against the candidate and dates the evidence from the mount event, never from the file. Stages 2 and 3 land separately.
